section.title: Final Warnings and Doxology
section.sectionRationale: Before he lays down his pen, Paul sounds a last warning: watch out for those who cause divisions contrary to the teaching you have learned, for they serve their own appetites and deceive the naive. He promises that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under their feet, sends greetings from his companions, and then lifts the whole letter into a soaring doxology to the God who is able to establish His people according to the gospel and the revealed mystery, to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ.
section.thesis: The gospel that saves must be guarded against those who divide and deceive, and the God who is able to establish His people by that gospel is the God of peace who will crush the serpent and receive everlasting glory through Jesus Christ.
section.frameNote: Three movements rising to a climax: a warning to watch out for and avoid those who cause divisions, with the promise that God will crush Satan; greetings from Paul's companions, including Tertius who wrote the letter down; and the closing doxology, the summit of the epistle, praising the God who establishes His people through the once hidden, now revealed gospel.

units.label: Watch out for those who cause divisions
units.note: avoid the deceivers who serve their own appetites

verses.text: Now I urge you, brothers, to watch out for those who create {{dichostasia|divisions}} and obstacles that are contrary to the teaching you have learned. Turn away from them.
For such people are not serving our Lord Christ, but their own appetites. By smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive.
Everyone has heard about your obedience, so I rejoice over you. But I want you to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil.
The God of peace will soon {{suntribo|crush}} Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

units.label: Greetings from Paul's companions
units.note: coworkers, kinsmen, and Tertius the scribe

verses.text: Timothy, my fellow worker, sends you greetings, as do Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my fellow countrymen.
I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord.
Gaius, who has hosted me and all the church, sends you greetings. Erastus, the city treasurer, sends you greetings, as does our brother Quartus.

units.label: The closing doxology
units.note: glory to the God who establishes us by the revealed mystery

verses.text: Now to Him who is able to strengthen you by my gospel and by the proclamation of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the {{mysterion|mystery}} concealed for ages past
but now revealed and made known through the writings of the prophets by the command of the eternal God, in order to lead all nations to the {{hypakoe|obedience}} that comes from faith,
to the only wise God be {{doxa|glory}} forever through Jesus Christ! Amen.

dichostasia.gloss: Division, dissension, a standing apart. Paul warns against those who create dichostasia contrary to the apostolic teaching, tearing the one body into factions. It names the work of those who wound the church's unity for the sake of their own agenda, and it is listed elsewhere among the works of the flesh.

suntribo.gloss: To crush, shatter, or break in pieces. Paul promises that the God of peace will soon suntribo Satan under the feet of His people, echoing the ancient promise that the seed of the woman would crush the serpent's head. The word carries the note of decisive, final victory over the enemy.

mysterion.gloss: A mystery, a truth once hidden in God and now disclosed. The doxology celebrates the mystery kept secret for long ages but now revealed in the gospel and made known to all nations. It is not a riddle to be solved but a secret purpose of God, unveiled in Christ, that Jew and Gentile alike are gathered into one saved people.

hypakoe.gloss: Obedience, a hearing that submits and trusts. The doxology aims at the obedience of faith among all nations, the very phrase with which the letter opened. The whole of Romans is bracketed by this goal: that the nations would come to the obedience that flows from faith in Christ.

doxa.gloss: Glory, weight, splendor, honor. The letter that began with the gospel of God ends by ascribing doxa to the only wise God forever through Jesus Christ. All the argument of Romans resolves into praise: salvation is from God and for God, and His is the everlasting glory.

basic.context: Paul closes his letter with a final pastoral warning, a round of greetings from those with him, and a magnificent doxology. Having spent the letter building up the church in the gospel, he now guards it against those who would divide and deceive it. Then, gathering up every theme of the epistle, he breaks into praise to the God who is able to establish His people by that same gospel.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the warning and the doxology together. The threat of division is real, but the last word is not danger; it is the God of peace who crushes Satan and the God of glory who establishes His people. The doxology deliberately echoes the letter's opening in Romans 1: the gospel promised through the prophets, the mystery now revealed, and the obedience of faith among all nations. It is the closing bracket of the whole book.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul warns against those who cause dichostasia, division, contrary to sound teaching. He promises that God will suntribo, crush, Satan underfoot. The doxology unveils the mysterion, the once hidden purpose of God, now revealed to bring the nations to the hypakoe of faith, the obedience Paul named in chapter one. It ends by ascribing doxa, glory, to the only wise God forever.
basic.typology: The promise that the God of peace will crush Satan under your feet reaches back to Genesis 3:15, where God foretold that the seed of the woman would crush the serpent's head. What was promised in Eden is accomplished in Christ and shared with His people. The mystery now revealed through the prophetic writings shows the whole Old Testament pointing forward to this unveiling in the gospel.
basic.christ: The doxology is offered through Jesus Christ, and the gospel it celebrates is the proclamation of Jesus Christ. He is the content of the mystery now revealed, the one in whom the nations are gathered, and the mediator through whom glory rises to God. The victory over Satan is His victory, won at the cross and shared with His people. Every strand of the letter is tied off in Him.
basic.god: The passage is God-centered from start to finish. He is the God of peace who crushes the enemy, the eternal God who commands the gospel to go to all nations, the only wise God who planned the mystery before the ages, and the God of glory who is able to establish His people. The letter that opened with the gospel of God closes with unending glory to God through Christ.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 3:15 promises that the woman's seed will crush the serpent's head, fulfilled as God crushes Satan under His people's feet. Romans 1:1-5 opens with the gospel promised through the prophets and the obedience of faith among the nations, which the doxology echoes. Ephesians 3:4-6 unfolds the mystery of Jew and Gentile made one. 1 Corinthians 14:33 calls Him the God of peace, not disorder.
basic.oneStory: The whole story of Scripture is gathered here. The serpent who struck in Eden is crushed under the feet of the redeemed. The mystery kept secret for long ages, that God would save the nations through His Son, is now revealed and preached to all peoples. The letter that opened with the gospel of God promised beforehand ends with glory to the only wise God, the story come full circle from promise to praise.

context.literary:
Romans 16:17 to 27 reads like a letter that has already said goodbye and then cannot stop. Paul has closed his long list of greetings in verses 1 to 16, and now he turns sharply, with the same verb of appeal he used to open his practical section in Romans 12:1, 'I urge you.' The passage then falls into three panels that mirror one another. Verses 17 to 20 hold a warning and a promise. Verses 21 to 23 hold greetings from the men around Paul. Verses 25 to 27 hold a single sentence of praise that runs without a full stop from 'Now to Him who is able' to 'Amen.'

The first panel is built on a contrast between two kinds of service. The troublemakers serve 'their own appetites,' verse 18, while the Romans' obedience is known everywhere, verse 19. Paul then balances two commands against each other, 'wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil.' The wisdom is directed toward the good and the innocence toward evil, which is the reverse of what the false teachers manage, since they are clever at flattery and gullible about their own motives.

The central promise of verse 20 is set in the future tense and carries the small adverb 'soon.' It falls right between a warning and a blessing, so that the church hears the danger and the victory in one breath.

The final sentence is a single long unit, and its shape is a chain of prepositional phrases, each adding one more reason for praise: according to my gospel, according to the revelation of the mystery, through the prophetic writings, by the command of the eternal God, for the obedience of faith among all nations. It begins with God's ability and ends with God's glory, and the whole epistle's vocabulary is gathered inside it. Scholars often point out that its last phrase, 'obedience that comes from faith,' is a deliberate frame with Romans 1:5, so that the letter is bracketed by the same words at its start and its finish.
context.historical:
Paul is most likely writing from Corinth, at the end of the three months he spent in Greece, Acts 20:2 to 3. The names in verses 21 to 23 fit that setting. Gaius, who 'has hosted me and all the church,' verse 23, is almost certainly the Gaius whom Paul baptized in Corinth, 1 Corinthians 1:14, and whose house was large enough to hold the whole congregation. Erastus is called the city treasurer, a civic officer with real standing in a Roman colony, and 2 Timothy 4:20 says that an Erastus stayed in Corinth. A paving inscription in Corinth that names an Erastus has often been linked to him, though that identification is debated.

Tertius is the one person in the letter who steps out of the dictation line. Paul normally spoke his letters to a scribe and added a closing greeting in his own hand, as in 1 Corinthians 16:21 and Galatians 6:11. Here the scribe adds his own hello, 'I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter,' verse 22. It is a small, human reminder that Romans, the most carefully argued letter in the New Testament, was taken down one sentence at a time by a named man.

Timothy is the familiar coworker of Acts 16:1. Jason may be the host of Acts 17:5 to 9 in Thessalonica, and Sosipater may be the Sopater of Berea in Acts 20:4, though Paul's phrase 'my fellow countrymen' only says they are Jews, so these identifications are probable and not certain.

The warning of verses 17 to 18 arrives in a church Paul had never visited. Rome's congregations met in homes, and the earlier part of the chapter names many of them. Such small house groups were exposed to travelling teachers who offered themselves as guests and then built a following. The 'smooth talk and flattery' of verse 18 describes a style familiar in a city that prized polished speech, and the 'naive' are those with no experience of how persuasion works.
context.canonical:
The promise that the God of peace will crush Satan is the New Testament's first deliberate echo of Genesis 3:15 outside the Gospels, though Paul does not quote it. The link rests on the picture of a foot over a serpent and not on borrowed wording. The same victorious foot appears in Psalm 110:1, 'until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet,' which the New Testament applies to Christ again and again. Paul's twist is that the feet belong to the church. The victory won by the head of the body is shared with the members.

The phrase 'God of peace' belongs to Paul's blessings across his letters, Romans 15:33, Philippians 4:9, 1 Thessalonians 5:23, and it fits the warning here, because the people he warns against are those who break peace.

The doxology draws on three streams. 'The mystery concealed for ages past' is the vocabulary of Ephesians 3:3 to 6 and Colossians 1:26 to 27, where the mystery is that Gentiles share in the promise. The 'writings of the prophets' echoes Romans 1:2 and 15:4, which say that the Scriptures were always pointing at this gospel. And 'to the only wise God be glory forever' is the family of 1 Timothy 1:17 and Jude 25, praise addressed to the one God who alone is God.

The paragraph also matters for the study of the letter's shape. As the BSB footnote on verse 27 observes, some manuscripts place these verses elsewhere, after Romans 14:23 or 15:33. The verses are accepted as Paul's own and are firmly part of the canonical letter, and the variation is a window into how early churches copied and read Romans, sometimes in shorter forms.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants the Roman believers to do three things at once and to see that they belong together. First, to keep their eyes open. The Greek verb he chooses means to look carefully at something in order to take its measure, and the object is a type of person, not a named party. He offers a test, not a name: do they cause obstacles to the teaching the Romans already received, and do they serve themselves? Second, to stay innocent. Paul does not want the church to become suspicious and hard, so he sets the call to watchfulness beside a call to purity of heart, and the promise of verse 20 is given to the whole assembly, not to a few heresy hunters. Third, to end by looking up. The greetings in verses 21 to 23 place the church among a wider family of coworkers, and the doxology lifts the reading from the earthly dangers of verses 17 to 18 to the God who stands over them.

The first hearers, a church of Jews and Gentiles who had recently seen tensions over food and festivals in chapters 14 and 15, would have heard the warning as a final seal on the unity Paul had been building. He does not name the people he has in mind, and that restraint is part of his intent: the pattern is what matters, and the church is meant to recognise it whenever it appears.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The list of names and the notice that Tertius took the dictation describe a moment in the life of the early church and carry no command beyond the courtesy of passing on greetings. The warning, by contrast, is written in the imperative, 'watch out' and 'turn away,' and the doxology is a pattern for worship. What applies today is the test Paul gives, whether a teacher puts obstacles in the way of the apostolic message, and whether he serves Christ or his own appetite. It does not authorise treating every disagreement as a danger. Paul himself accepts that believers differ over food and holy days in Romans 14, and he tells the strong and the weak to welcome one another. The divisive person of 16:17 is marked by the damage done to the shared teaching, not by holding a different opinion on a matter of freedom.

The promise of verse 20 is a statement about what God will do, not an instruction to wage war. Believers share in the victory by staying faithful and by letting the God of peace do the crushing.

debates.question: How should the church treat those who cause divisions contrary to sound teaching?

views.label: Mark and avoid them
views.case: Paul says plainly to watch out for them and turn away, refusing them a platform, since they serve their own appetites and deceive the naive with smooth talk; the church protects its unity and its members by not entertaining such teaching.

views.label: Engage and correct patiently first
views.case: Others stress that elsewhere Paul urges gentle correction of opponents in hope of repentance, so avoidance follows only after patient warning has failed; the aim is always the health of the body and, if possible, the recovery of the erring.

debates.bearing: Both agree the divisive teaching must not be allowed to spread and that the flock must be guarded; the historic pastoral practice is to warn clearly, seek repentance, and separate from those who persist in dividing the church against the apostolic gospel.

debates.question: Where do the verses of the doxology belong, given the manuscript variations?

views.label: The original close of the letter
views.case: The best reading places verses 25 to 27 here as the fitting climax, echoing the opening of Romans and rounding off the epistle with praise; this is where most manuscripts and modern editions set them.

views.label: A moveable ending in some copies
views.case: Some manuscripts locate the doxology after chapter 14 or 15, likely reflecting early liturgical or editorial use, and a few omit it; but this does not unsettle its authenticity or its fitness as the letter's conclusion.

debates.bearing: However the copies arrange it, the doxology is received as the true and fitting end of Romans, gathering the letter's themes into glory to God through Jesus Christ; the variation touches placement, not the gospel it proclaims.

debates.question: Who are the people Paul warns about in verses 17 and 18?

views.label: Judaizing teachers
views.case: Some think of the men who dogged Paul's steps insisting that Gentiles keep the law, as in Galatians. The language of 'obstacles' and 'the teaching you have learned' fits a challenge to what Paul had taught about grace, and the dispute over law runs through Romans.

views.label: Libertines who made grace a licence
views.case: Others point to Romans 6:1, where Paul answers those who said, 'Let us continue in sin so that grace may increase,' and to 'their own appetites' in verse 18. On this view the danger is a gospel that excuses indulgence.

views.label: A type, not a party
views.case: A third reading notes that Paul names no group and gives no doctrine, only two marks, the effect on the church and the motive. He may be describing a recurring kind of teacher in any age, whatever the particular error.

debates.bearing: Paul's own description is limited to the damage done and the motive behind it, so the passage works as a test to be applied with care and cannot be turned into a licence to label opponents. All three readings agree that what is at stake is the shared apostolic teaching.

debates.question: Do verses 25 to 27 belong at the end of Romans?

views.label: Original and in its place
views.case: The vocabulary of the doxology matches the letter's opening and its main themes, the obedience of faith, the prophetic writings, the revealed purpose of God, and the great majority of manuscripts and modern editions keep it here. The doxology is a fitting climax.

views.label: Moved or added later in some copies
views.case: The BSB footnote records that some manuscripts place the verses after Romans 14:23 or after 15:33. Some scholars have thought this reflects shorter forms of the letter that circulated, with the doxology moving as the final chapters were added or removed.

debates.bearing: Even those who take the variation seriously treat the doxology as Pauline in thought, and the weight of the evidence keeps it at the end. The practical result is the same: the letter ends in praise to the God it has been describing.

study.originalLanguages:
Four Greek words in this passage carry more weight than English shows. The first is the verb Paul uses for 'watch out,' skopeo, from which English takes 'scope.' It means to fix the eyes on something in order to judge it, and Paul uses the same verb in Philippians 3:17 for 'carefully observing' those who walk by his pattern. The identical verb serves for imitating the good and detecting the harmful, which tells us that watchfulness here is attention, and the object decides whether the attention leads to following or to turning away. The companion verb 'turn away,' ekklino, is the one Paul used in Romans 3:12, 'All have turned away,' so the church is told to take a step in the opposite direction from the one humanity took from God.

The second word is the pair that describes the manner of the deceivers, chrestologia and eulogia, rendered 'smooth talk and flattery.' Chrestologia is speech that sounds kind and useful, a pleasant voice, and eulogia, which usually means a blessing in the New Testament, here carries a fair-sounding, flattering sense. The same Greek word for 'blessing' therefore appears for false teachers' compliments and for the true praise of the doxology's God, and the contrast is deliberate. The audience of this talk is 'the naive,' akakoi, people without malice, whose own guilelessness is the opening the deceivers use.

The third word is akeraioi, 'innocent,' literally 'unmixed' or 'unadulterated,' the word Jesus uses in Matthew 10:16, 'as innocent as doves.' Matthew's sentence sets this beside 'shrewd as snakes,' and Paul's version in verse 19 is its close cousin, wise about the good and unmixed with evil. The idea of purity as lack of admixture suits a passage about teaching diluted with self-interest.

The fourth is the verb in the final panel, sterizo, 'to strengthen.' Paul used it in Romans 1:11 when he wrote of his longing to impart a gift 'to strengthen you,' and he comes back to the same word in verse 25. The reader who notices the echo sees that what Paul wished to do by visiting, God is able to do by the gospel. The infinitive after 'able' also has a grammar worth noting: 'Now to Him who is able' is the opening of a dative of praise whose main verb is never expressed, so the whole thing is an exclamation, a sentence that exists only to give God the last word.

The fifth feature is in verse 20. The verb 'will crush,' suntripsei, is future tense, and it is joined to the adverb en tachei, 'soon' or 'quickly.' The word can mean swiftly as well as soon, and the New Testament uses the phrase for events that are near in the speaker's horizon, so the promise has urgency in either sense. The phrase 'under your feet' is plural, so every member of the church receives a share in the victory.

typology.type: The foot on the serpent, Genesis 3:15 and Psalm 110:1
typology.fulfillment: Genesis 3:15 promised a conflict between the woman's offspring and the serpent in which the offspring would strike the head. Paul does not quote it, but he plainly has the image in mind when he says God will crush Satan 'under your feet.' The correspondence is in the posture of triumph, a heel set on a defeated enemy, and in the surprise that the offspring is now plural, since the whole church shares in what the Head has won, Romans 8:17. Psalm 110:1 gives the enemy a footstool, and Hebrews 2:14 describes how that victory came by death. The type is not yet exhausted: Revelation 20:10 places the final end of the devil still ahead, so the promise of 'soon' is already begun and yet unfinished.

typology.type: The mystery that God reveals, Daniel 2
typology.fulfillment: In Daniel 2:28 the prophet tells Nebuchadnezzar, 'there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries.' A mystery in that sense is a divine purpose that no human wisdom can reach and that God discloses at the time He chooses. Paul takes that pattern and applies it to the plan that all nations would be brought to God. The correspondence is that the secret is real, that it belongs to God, and that it is revealed by His initiative. What is new is the scope. Daniel's mysteries concern kingdoms that rise and fall; Paul's concerns the Gentiles' entrance into the promise, Ephesians 3:6, now revealed through Christ and 'made known through the writings of the prophets.'

typology.type: The nations coming in, Psalm 22 and Genesis 12
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament holds a steady promise that the nations will turn to God. Genesis 12:3 says that all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham, and Psalm 22:27 says that 'all the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the LORD.' The doxology says that the revealed purpose is 'to lead all nations to the obedience that comes from faith.' The type is the prophesied ingathering; the fulfilment is its beginning in the preaching of Christ and the spread of the gospel among Gentiles in Paul's own ministry. The pattern falls short until Revelation 7:9, where the multitude from every nation stands before the throne, which shows that the work of verse 26 is still moving toward its completion.

typology.type: The closing praise of the Psalter
typology.fulfillment: Each of the first four books of the Psalms ends with a blessing of God and an Amen, Psalm 41:13, 72:18 to 19, 89:52 and 106:48, and the whole collection closes with a final burst of praise in Psalm 150. Israel's own songbook was shaped to end in worship, and Paul's letter ends the same way, with a blessing to God and 'Amen.' Psalm 72:19 asks that the whole earth be filled with His glory, and Paul's final line, 'to the only wise God be glory forever,' answers that prayer by turning theology into song. The correspondence lies in form and in aim. What the earlier doxologies hoped for in Israel's king, Paul gives 'through Jesus Christ.'

study.christ:
Christ appears in this passage at the beginning, the middle and the end, always with a different job. At the beginning he is the one whose servants the false teachers are not. 'They are not serving our Lord Christ,' Paul says, and the phrase makes the rival allegiance explicit, since the choice offered to every teacher is between serving Christ and serving the belly. Philippians 3:18 to 19 describes people who live as 'enemies of the cross of Christ,' whose 'god is their belly,' and the two passages interpret each other. A teacher who gathers a following for himself has replaced the Lord he claims to serve.

In the middle he is the Lord of the grace that closes the warning. 'The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you,' verse 20, is more than a blessing. Placed immediately after the promise of victory, it says that the means of the church's survival is Christ's own favour, which carries them. The victory over Satan is promised to the church, but the grace is Christ's, and the church wins by receiving it.

At the end he is both the content of the preaching and the channel of the praise. 'The proclamation of Jesus Christ,' verse 25, is the name Paul gives to the thing he preaches, and it stands beside 'my gospel' as an equal description. The phrase can mean the proclamation that is about Christ, or the proclamation that Christ himself makes through his messengers, and Paul may well intend both. Either way, the purpose of God hidden for ages is now fastened to a person. The 'mystery' is not an abstract principle but the one Colossians 1:27 calls 'Christ in you, the hope of glory.'

The doxology ends 'through Jesus Christ,' and the preposition matters. Christ is the mediator by whom creatures give glory to God, as Hebrews 13:15 says, 'through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise.' No one comes to praise the only wise God except through him, and the praise itself is made possible by what he accomplished.

There is also a pattern link to the promise about crushing. Hebrews 2:14 explains how it is fulfilled, through His death, and 1 John 3:8 says that the Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil. The way the church shares in that victory is by being united to the one who won it, and Romans 8:37 says believers are 'more than conquerors through Him who loved us.' It would be forced to find Christ in Tertius's pen or in Erastus's office, and the passage does not ask for that. The Christ it presents is the Lord served, the grace received and the one through whom praise ascends.
study.god:
The passage names God in four ways, and each one explains the others. He is 'the God of peace' in verse 20. In Paul's letters this title belongs to the God who reconciles, Romans 15:33 and Philippians 4:9, and it is set in a verse about conflict because peace in Scripture is not the absence of struggle but the result of God's rule. The one who gives peace is the one who defeats what breaks it. A church that is threatened by divisive talk is promised the God who has the power to end the division at its source.

He is the God who is 'able,' verse 25. Paul has already used the idea in Romans 4:21, where Abraham was fully convinced that God 'was able to do what He had promised,' and in 14:4, where the weak believer will stand because 'the Lord is able to make him stand.' The strength of the church rests on an ability that belongs to God and not on the vigilance of the believers. The warning of verses 17 to 18 therefore stands inside a larger assurance, and it does not turn the church into the guardian of its own survival.

He is the 'eternal God,' who commands. The phrase 'by the command of the eternal God' puts the spread of the gospel under a divine order, not a human project. The mission to the nations is not a plan Paul drew up. It is an order from the God who stands outside time, who concealed the mystery for ages and chose the hour to reveal it. That gives the missionary calling a firmness and a patience at once: firmness, because it is commanded, and patience, because it follows His timetable.

He is the 'only wise God.' Wisdom here is God's way of ordering history so that the hidden thing comes to light at the right time and through the right means, the prophets' writings and the apostles' proclamation. The word 'only' says that no rival source of wisdom stands beside Him, which fits the whole letter from Romans 1:22, where those who claimed to be wise became fools, to 11:33, where Paul cries out at 'the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God.' It also stands against the deceivers of verse 18, whose clever talk is wisdom of the wrong kind.

The tension the passage holds is between divine certainty and human watchfulness. God will crush Satan, and still the Romans must watch out and turn away. God is able to strengthen them, and still Paul wants them wise about good. The Bible keeps both truths together, and the passage shows how: the commands are the means by which the promise is worked out, and the promise is what makes the commands bearable.

For worship, the passage teaches that the right end of theology is praise offered to God alone. The letter does not end with a summary of arguments or a call to action but with an 'Amen,' as if the whole long argument were a single act of adoration. Praise is the proper response to a God who is peace-giving, able, eternal and wise, and who has made Himself known.

crossReferences.note: The promise that the woman's offspring would strike the serpent's head sits behind verse 20. Paul does not quote it but takes up its image of a foot upon the enemy, and he widens the circle, since the victory belongs to the whole church and not to one lone champion. Reading the two verses together shows that the first promise of Scripture is still being kept at the end of Romans.

The letter opens with the gospel promised beforehand through the prophets in the Holy Scriptures, and with a mission 'to call all those among the Gentiles to the obedience that comes from faith.' The doxology picks up each element, the prophets, the nations and the obedience of faith, and closes the circle. Paul is deliberately framing the whole letter with one idea.

Paul longed to visit Rome to impart a gift 'to strengthen you,' and he used the same verb that begins the doxology. The echo shows that what he could not yet do in person, God is able to do by the gospel. The closing praise answers the opening longing and turns Paul's wish into a confidence in God.

Paul explains the mystery of Christ as something not made known in earlier generations but now revealed to the apostles and prophets by the Spirit, that Gentiles are fellow heirs of the same body. Romans 16:25 to 26 compresses the same thought and shows that the idea of a hidden plan now revealed was a settled part of his teaching.

The mystery is 'hidden for ages and generations' and is now disclosed to the saints, and it is identified as 'Christ in you, the hope of glory.' This parallel turns the abstract word of Romans 16:25 into a person and shows that the mystery is the presence of Christ among the nations.

Paul warns about people who live as 'enemies of the cross of Christ' and whose 'god is their belly.' The belly image is behind 'their own appetites' in Romans 16:18. The two passages show the same recognition mark of false teaching, a ministry that serves the teacher's comfort, and the same tears of a pastor who sees it.

Jesus sends His disciples out among wolves and tells them to be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves. Paul's call to be wise about the good and innocent about evil in Romans 16:19 is the same balanced instruction, carried from the mission field into the life of the church.

Paul tells Titus to reject a divisive person after a first and second warning. This is the fuller procedure that stands behind the shorter instruction in Romans 16:17, and it shows that turning away comes after patient admonition. The two verses together prevent the Roman command from being read as a quick ban.

A believer who ignores the apostolic word is to be noted and not associated with, so that he may be ashamed, yet he is not to be treated as an enemy but warned as a brother. The aim of distance is restoration, and the passage gives the spirit in which Romans 16:17 should be carried out.

Paul baptized Gaius in Corinth, and Gaius is the host named in Romans 16:23. The letter to Rome was therefore written from the home of a man whose own baptism Paul recalls in the letter to Corinth, and the link helps to fix where and when Romans was dictated.

Jude closes with the same pattern of praise: to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling, glory and majesty, now and forever, Amen. Two New Testament letters end by looking away from the dangers they have named to the God who is able, and this shows how the early church closed its writing with worship.

The promise that Satan will be crushed has its explanation here: the Son shared flesh and blood so that through His death He might destroy the one who holds the power of death. The soon-coming victory of Romans 16:20 is not a new event but the outworking of the cross.

study.oneStory:
Romans 16 closes a letter that began with the problem of sin and the question of how God can be righteous in saving sinners. Chapters 1 to 3 show the whole world guilty, chapters 4 and 5 the answer by faith, chapters 6 to 8 the new life in the Spirit, chapters 9 to 11 the place of Israel, and chapters 12 to 15 the common life of the church. This final passage gathers every one of those threads into a few lines and sets them against the enemy who stands behind all of them.

The promise of verse 20 reaches back to the first judgment in Eden. The serpent's sentence in Genesis 3:15 foretold a defeat, and the Old Testament waited for the one who would bring it. By the time Paul writes, the head has been bruised at the cross, Colossians 2:15, and the church lives between that decisive victory and its full display, which is the meaning of 'soon.' The promise is made to believers who still face deceivers and still need to watch.

The revealed mystery reaches back to Abraham, to whom God said that all the families of the earth would be blessed. For centuries the promise sat inside Israel's story and inside the prophets' writings, and its full scope was hidden, as Paul says, 'for ages past.' Now the Gentiles are being led into the obedience of faith, and the letter's closing greeting list, with its Jewish and Gentile names side by side, is a small living picture of the answer.

The passage also looks forward. The warning shows that the church will go on facing teachers who serve themselves until the Lord returns, 2 Peter 2:1 to 3. The doxology looks forward to a day when the praise that is now offered by a scattered group of house churches will be offered by a countless multitude, Revelation 7:9 to 10, and when the one who 'is able' will have finished what He began.

In the new creation the warnings will have no place, because the deceiver is gone, Revelation 20:10, and the divisions that wounded the church will be healed, since the nations will walk by the light of the city and bring into it their glory, Revelation 21:24. Paul's 'Amen' is the first line of a song that has no final line. The story that began with a hidden plan ends with the plan fully known and every voice joined in the praise of the only wise God.

quiz.q: What does Paul tell the Romans to do about those who cause divisions contrary to sound teaching?

options.text: Watch out for them and turn away from them, for they serve their own appetites.
options.note: Paul urges vigilance and avoidance, since such people deceive the naive and serve themselves, not Christ.

options.text: Appoint them as leaders to keep the peace.
options.note: Paul says to avoid them, not to give them authority.

options.text: Ignore them entirely and never warn anyone.
options.note: Paul does say to turn away, but not to stay silent; he warns the church clearly before telling them to avoid such people.

options.text: Adopt their teaching to preserve unity.
options.note: Unity is a real concern, but their teaching is contrary to what the church learned; adopting it would be the very division Paul warns against.

quiz.q: What does Paul promise the God of peace will soon do?

options.text: Crush Satan under the feet of His people.
options.note: Paul promises decisive victory, echoing the promise of Genesis 3:15.

options.text: Remove all hardship from their lives at once.
options.note: God does bring peace and victory, but the specific promise here is the crushing of Satan, not the immediate end of all trials.

options.text: Leave the enemy undefeated forever.
options.note: This concerns Satan, but says the opposite of the promise: God will crush him underfoot.

options.text: Reward the divisive teachers.
options.note: God crushes the enemy; He does not reward those who serve their own appetites.

quiz.q: Who is Tertius, mentioned in the greetings?

options.text: The scribe who wrote down the letter as Paul dictated it.
options.note: Tertius identifies himself as the one who wrote the letter down, adding his own greeting in the Lord.

options.text: The city treasurer of Corinth.
options.note: That is Erastus, also named in the greetings; Tertius is the one who wrote the letter down.

options.text: The founder of the Roman church.
options.note: No single person is credited with founding the Roman church; Tertius is the scribe, not its founder.

options.text: A false teacher Paul is warning against.
options.note: Tertius is a brother greeting the church in the Lord, not an opponent.

quiz.q: In the doxology, how is the gospel described in relation to the ages past?

options.text: As a mystery concealed for ages but now revealed and made known to all nations.
options.note: The doxology celebrates the once hidden mystery now disclosed through the prophetic writings to the nations.

options.text: As a brand new idea with no roots in the Scriptures.
options.note: It is made known through the writings of the prophets; it is not rootless.

options.text: As a secret that remains hidden from everyone.
options.note: The mystery is now revealed and made known to all nations.

options.text: As a message only for one nation.
options.note: It is now revealed, but made known to all nations to bring the obedience of faith, not to one nation only.

quiz.q: How does the letter finally end, and to whom is glory given?

options.text: To the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ.
options.note: The doxology ascribes everlasting glory to the only wise God through Jesus Christ.

options.text: To the Roman church, for its faithfulness.
options.note: Paul does rejoice in their obedience, but the glory is given to God alone, not to the church.

options.text: To Paul, for writing such a great letter.
options.note: Paul is the writer, but he directs all glory to God, not to himself.

options.text: To the wisdom of the age.
options.note: Glory is given to the only wise God, not to human or worldly wisdom.

questions: Paul warns against those who cause divisions with smooth talk and flattery. How can you grow more discerning, wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil, without becoming cynical?
The God of peace promises to crush Satan under His people's feet. How does this echo of Eden's promise strengthen you when you feel the enemy's pressure?
Tertius, the scribe, and many unnamed helpers made this letter possible. Where might God be calling you to serve faithfully in a supporting role that others may never notice?
The doxology celebrates a mystery once hidden but now revealed to all nations. How does it move you to know that God planned your salvation before the ages and has now made it known?
The letter ends with glory to God forever through Jesus Christ. How would ordering your life around the glory of God, rather than your own, reshape your priorities this week?

translationNotes.note: The promise that the God of peace will crush Satan under your feet deliberately echoes Genesis 3:15, the promise that the woman's seed would crush the serpent's head, now shared with Christ's people.
The earliest manuscripts do not include verse 24, a repeated grace benediction; it appears in the footnotes of many editions and is omitted here, so the numbering moves from verse 23 to verse 25.
The obedience that comes from faith renders the same phrase found in Romans 1:5, framing the whole letter. The sentence of the doxology runs on into verse 27.
